questions.q: What does it mean for a matrix A to be Hermitian?
options: A equals its own transpose, with no conjugation required
A is invertible and has determinant equal to 1
A equals its own conjugate transpose: A = A^dagger
Every entry of A is a real number
questions.explain: Hermitian means A = A^dagger, where A^dagger is formed by transposing A and conjugating every entry. This requires a real diagonal and off-diagonal entries that are conjugates of each other -- not that every entry of A itself is real.

questions.q: For A = [[2, 1-2i], [1+2i, -1]], why is A Hermitian?
options: Because every entry in the matrix is a real number
Because the determinant of A happens to equal zero
Because A is symmetric when you ignore the imaginary parts
Both diagonal entries (2 and -1) are real, and the off-diagonal entries 1-2i and 1+2i are conjugates of each other
questions.explain: Checking A = A^dagger requires a real diagonal (2 and -1 both qualify) and off-diagonal entries that mirror each other under conjugation: (1-2i)* = 1+2i, which matches A_21 exactly.

questions.q: For B = [[1, 2+i], [3-i, 4]], why is B NOT Hermitian, even though both diagonal entries are real?
options: B is not Hermitian because its diagonal entries are not both real
B is actually Hermitian; a real diagonal is sufficient on its own
B cannot be Hermitian because it has an odd number of nonzero entries
The off-diagonal entries fail the conjugate test: (2+i)* = 2-i, which does not equal B_21 = 3-i
questions.explain: A real diagonal is necessary but not sufficient. The off-diagonal pair must also satisfy A_12 = (A_21)*. Here (2+i)* = 2-i, which does not match B_21 = 3-i, so B fails the Hermitian test despite its real diagonal.

questions.q: For the Hermitian matrix A = [[2, 1-2i], [1+2i, -1]], its trace is 1 and its determinant is -7. What does solving for the eigenvalues confirm?
options: The eigenvalues are complex numbers with nonzero imaginary parts
The eigenvalues are (1 + sqrt(29))/2 and (1 - sqrt(29))/2, both real numbers, consistent with A being Hermitian
The eigenvalues cannot be computed because A has complex entries
The eigenvalues are both equal to the trace, 1
questions.explain: Solving lambda^2 - lambda - 7 = 0 gives lambda = (1 +/- sqrt(1+28))/2 = (1 +/- sqrt(29))/2, two distinct real numbers -- confirming the theorem that Hermitian matrices always have real eigenvalues, regardless of complex entries elsewhere in the matrix.

questions.q: Why must quantum observables (energy, spin, position) be represented by Hermitian operators rather than arbitrary matrices?
options: Hermitian matrices are always equal to the identity matrix, which simplifies calculations

A measurement's possible outcomes are the operator's eigenvalues, and a physical measurement result must be a real number -- Hermitian matrices are exactly the matrices guaranteed to have only real eigenvalues
Non-Hermitian matrices cannot be multiplied by vectors
Hermitian matrices are the only matrices that have an inverse
questions.explain: Measurement outcomes correspond to an observable's eigenvalues, and a real measuring device cannot report a complex number. Hermitian matrices are precisely the matrices whose eigenvalues are guaranteed real, which is why observables are modeled as Hermitian operators.
